1: # AGENTS.md — 02_Knowledge
2: 
3: Structured reference notes on tech concepts, syntax guides, and foundational theory.
4: 
5: ## Why have knowledge notes?
6: 
7: - **Reference**: something to come back to when deploying or troubleshooting
8: - **Learning**: writing things down solidifies understanding
9: - **Research input**: Knowledge is the foundation that Research builds upon
10: - **Onboarding**: a single place to understand how things work
11: 
12: ## When to create
13: 
14: After an idea is promoted, or whenever you learn something worth documenting.
15: 
16: ## Status Lifecycle
17: 
18: ```
19: draft → accepted
20:   L__> archived → (move to 06_Archive/knowledge/)
21: ```
22: 
23: - **draft**: Outline or incomplete
24: - **accepted**: Reviewed and finalized
25: - **archived**: Stale or superseded
26: 
27: ## File system layout
28: 
29: ```
30: 02_Knowledge/
31: └── technologies/
32:     ├── tools/           # CLI tools, software utilities
33:     ├── services/        # specific services (forgejo, homepage, etc.)
34:     ├── kubernetes/      # k8s concepts, patterns, manifests
35:     └── hardware/        # physical hardware, specs, diagrams
36: ```
37: 
38: All names in kebab-case. Each topic is a folder with atomic notes inside. Max 3 levels deep.
39: 
40: ## Frontmatter (required)
41: 
42: ```yaml
43: ---
44: title: ""
45: status: draft        # draft | accepted | archived
46: author: ""
47: date: YYYY-MM-DD
48: tags: []
49: sources:
50:   - url: ""
51:     title: ""
52: last_audit_date: YYYY-MM-DD
53: related_docs: []
54: ---
55: ```
56: 
57: Example:
58: 
59: ```yaml
60: ---
61: title: "Ingress controllers in Kubernetes"
62: status: draft
63: author: "padawont"
64: date: 2026-08-13
65: tags: [kubernetes, networking, ingress]
66: sources:
67:   - url: "https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/ingress/"
68:     title: "Kubernetes Ingress docs"
69: last_audit_date: 2026-08-13
70: related_docs:
71:   - "./05_Implementations/node-main/traefik/overview.md"
72: ---
73: ```
74: 
75: See `./Templates/knowledge/note.md` for a copyable template.
76: 
77: ## Structure
78: 
79: ```
80: # Title
81: 
82: Overview — what is this concept? Why does it matter?
83: 
84: ## Details
85: 
86: Deep dive with examples.
87: 
88: ## Sources / Further Reading
89: ```
90: 
91: Example — abstract:
92: 
93: ```yaml
94: # simplified, vendor-neutral
95: apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
96: kind: Ingress
97: metadata: { name: example-ingress }
98: spec:
99:   rules:
100:     - host: example.com
101:       http: { paths: [{ path: /, pathType: Prefix }] }
102: ```
103: 
104: Example — real config from node-main:
105: 
106: ```yaml
107: # actual running config, may drift from this doc
108: apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
109: kind: Ingress
110: metadata: { name: forgejo-ingress, namespace: forgejo }
111: spec:
112:   ingressClassName: traefik
113:   rules:
114:     - host: git.homelab.local
115:       http: { paths: [{ path: /, pathType: Prefix }] }
116: ```
117: 
118: ## Conventions
119: 
120: - **Atomic notes**: one concept per file. When a file hits 150 lines (including frontmatter and blank lines), split it.
121: - Both abstract examples and real configs are welcome — label each block as "Example — abstract" or "Example — real config"
122: - Set `last_audit_date` on every edit; re-audit weekly
123: - Use `related_docs` to cross-link to implementations and vice-versa
124: 
125: ## Agent Behaviour
126: 
127: | Role | May | Must not |
128: |---|---|---|
129: | `worker` | read, gather sources, create and edit the note | edit files outside its brief, add unsourced claims |
130: | `reviewer` | run all five review types, emit the JSON report | edit, propose unverified fixes |
131: | `editor` | revise the note and its JSON with a cited source or rule | change anything without a citation |
132: | `spec-writer` | append a spec section referencing this note | rewrite or delete note content |
133: | `cluster-worker` | not applicable to this folder | run operational plans here |
134: 
135: Review types: `source`, `accuracy`, `scope`, `structure`, `overlap`.
136: Escalation: anything unresolved goes to the hub in the handoff `blocked:` field — never a guess.

23: # Forgejo operations — backup, restore, upgrades
24: 
25: ## Overview
26: 
27: Day-to-day operations for a self-hosted Forgejo instance: consistent backups
28: with `forgejo dump` (or snapshotting), safe upgrades between releases, and
29: restore/verification. Forgejo follows semantic versioning since 7.0.0, and the
30: database stores its schema version so a downgrade is refused automatically.
31: 
32: ## Details
33: 
34: ### Backup
35: 
36: The reliable option is a synchronized point-in-time snapshot of all storage
37: Forgejo uses. On k3s that means snapshotting the Longhorn volume
38: (`./02_Knowledge/technologies/kubernetes/longhorn/storage.md`); if storage is
39: spread across several systems (DB on one volume, repos on another), stop
40: Forgejo during the backup so the pieces stay consistent.
41: 
42: For a simple single-filesystem setup the built-in command is:
43: 
44: ```bash
45: forgejo dump
46: ```
47: 
48: - Produces a single zip containing configuration, repositories, and the
49:   database.
50: - SQLite is already included in the zip; for PostgreSQL/MySQL also take a
51:   native `pg_dump`/`mysqldump` — the SQL dump embedded by `forgejo dump` has
52:   known bugs when re-injected into a new database.
53: - Schedule it as a k8s CronJob writing to a backup location (e.g. a separate
54:   volume or object storage), keeping a few rotations.
55: 
56: ### Restore
57: 
58: 1. Stop Forgejo.
59: 2. Extract the dump zip and restore data, repos, and config to the data volume.
60: 3. Restore the native database dump (for Postgres/MySQL).
61: 4. Start Forgejo and verify:
62:    `forgejo doctor check --all --log-file /tmp/doctor.log`
63:    plus a manual web-UI walk-through (login, a repo, an issue).
64: 
65: ### Upgrades
66: 
67: Forgejo release lifecycle:
68: 
69: | Channel | Support |
70: |---|---|
71: | **Stable** (latest) | Bugfix + security fixes for ~3 months + 2-week overlap |
72: | **LTS** (version published the first quarter of every year) | Critical fixes for ~1 year 3 months |
73: | **Experimental** (dev) | Not for production |
74: 
75: Upgrade procedure:
76: 
77: 1. **Back up first** — required when moving across a stable release, wise for
78:    minor/patch.
79: 2. Read the release notes for the target version, including known problematic
80:    upgrade paths (see the upgrade guide).
81: 3. Before switching: `forgejo manager flush-queues` (queued data is not
82:    guaranteed compatible between versions).
83: 4. Perform the upgrade by replacing the container image or binary — migrations
84:    run automatically on first start.
85: 5. **Verify carefully**: `forgejo doctor check --all` plus a manual checklist.
86:    A restore after an upgrade is easy; fixing a live instance weeks later is not.
87: 
88: Notes:
89: 
90: - Major version jumps (e.g. 15 → 16) may contain breaking changes and require
91:   the manual procedure; upgrading X → X+1 needs human verification. Staying on
92:   the `16` image tag gives minor updates automatically.
93: - Docker installs need docker >= 20.10.6.
94: - The database version guard refuses to start a downgraded binary against a
95:   newer database — do not bypass it.
96: - Subscribe to the security-announcements repo to plan security releases.
97: 
98: ### Day-to-day
99: 
100: - Logs: k8s — `kubectl logs -f deploy/forgejo -n forgejo`; Forgejo can also
101:   write logs to files via `[log]` sections (console/file modes); SQL logging
102:   is toggled by `LOG_SQL=true` in the `[database]` section.
103: - Health: rely on pod liveness/readiness probes hitting the web port; run
104:   `forgejo doctor` after any upgrade.
105: - Cross-check storage usage on the Longhorn PVC periodically.
106: 
107: ## Sources / Further Reading

109: - Upgrade guide: https://forgejo.org/docs/latest/admin/upgrade/

112: - Logging configuration: https://forgejo.org/docs/latest/admin/troubleshooting/logging/

19: # Migrating repositories to Forgejo
20: 
21: ## Overview
22: 
23: Repositories can be brought into Forgejo either as a **one-shot migration** (a
24: copy of the code plus issues, PRs, and releases) or as a **mirror** (kept in
25: sync with the source). One-shot migrations and pull mirrors start from the web
26: UI's migration flow; push mirrors are configured per-repository. Migrations
27: and mirrors work with GitHub, Gitea, GitLab, Gogs, and plain URLs. Migration
28: is how a homelab
29: instance adopts an existing GitHub/Gitea history instead of starting from an
30: empty repo.
31: 
32: ## Details
33: 
34: ### One-shot migration
35: 
36: - Go to **Create → New Migration** and pick the source:
37:   GitHub, Gitea, GitLab, Gogs, or a generic git URL.
38: - Authenticate with a token (see `./02_Knowledge/technologies/services/forgejo/security.md`
39:   for fine-grained token scopes) — for GitHub, docs recommend a fine-grained
40:   personal access token with Content read.
41: - Choose what to bring over: repository itself, issues, pull requests, releases,
42:   milestones, labels, wiki. PR/issue comments are filtered according to the
43:   selected migration options.
44: - Migration runs server-side; for large or LFS-heavy repositories the `[git]`
45:   timeout settings (config cheat sheet) may need raising.
46: 
47: ### Mirrors (continuous sync)
48: 
49: - A **pull mirror** re-fetches the source repository on a schedule
50:   (default `[mirror]` interval), keeping code, branches, and tags in sync.
51: - A **push mirror** pushes a Forgejo repo to a remote (e.g. GitHub) — by
52:   default it uses `git push --mirror` (all branches and tags); an optional
53:   branch filter restricts which branches are pushed. This is useful when
54:   Forgejo is canonical but an external copy is still published.
55: - Pull mirroring is chosen at repository creation (New Migration + the 'This
56:   repository will be a mirror' checkbox); push mirrors are set in **Settings →
57:   Repository → Mirror Settings**.
58: - A repository cannot be converted into a pull mirror after creation, and a
59:   push mirror force-pushes — it overwrites any changes on the remote.
60: 
61: ### Practical migration checklist
62: 
63: - **Tokens first**: generate a scoped token on the source and a Forgejo access
64:   token for API/CLI work afterwards.
65: - **LFS / large files**: verify Git LFS content transfers; LFS objects are not
66:   mirrored over SSH push mirrors. If the source blocks it, clone + push the
67:   LFS objects manually.
68: - **Wiki and packages**: not every source migrates these cleanly — move them
69:   separately (export/import) if needed.
70: - **Releases and tags**: confirm tags arrive; a re-tag can be done from a local
71:   clone if the migration missed some.
72: - **Old URLs**: GitHub mirrors may be kept alive; or add DNS/web redirects so
73:   existing links still resolve.
74: - **Users and orgs**: repo-level migrations bring author names/commits as-is;
75:   account/org structure is recreated on Forgejo manually.
76: 
77: ### Upgrade-path note
78: 
79: Forgejo also documents upgrades **from Gitea** (up to v1.22 included) as a
80: two-step path: any Gitea ≤ v1.22.x → Forgejo v10.0.x, then v10.0.x → any newer
81: Forgejo (e.g. v16). This is an instance upgrade, not a repo migration — see the
82: upgrade guide's from-Gitea section and `./02_Knowledge/technologies/services/forgejo/operations.md`.

86: - Repository mirrors (pull/push): https://forgejo.org/docs/latest/user/repo-mirror/
87: - Migration internals (service layout, comment filtering): https://forgejo.org/docs/latest/contributor/repository-migration/

25: # Installing and configuring Forgejo
26: 
27: ## Overview
28: 
29: Forgejo ships as a container image (`codeberg.org/forgejo/forgejo`) or a binary
30: distribution. On k3s it deploys as a Deployment with a Longhorn PVC, a Service
31: (`forgejo-http`, port 3000), and a Traefik Ingress at `git.homelab.local`.
32: Configuration lives in `app.ini` (created by the image on first start) and can
33: be overridden via `FORGEJO__[SECTION]__[KEY]` env vars.
34: 
35: > Not deployed yet — all manifests below are **Example — abstract**, not live config.
36: 
37: ## Details
38: 
39: ### Container image
40: 
41: ```bash
42: docker pull codeberg.org/forgejo/forgejo:16
43: ```
44: 
45: - The `16` tag tracks the latest minor release of the v16 line; `16.0` tracks
46:   the latest patch. Swap `codeberg.org` for the mirror `data.forgejo.org`.
47: - Rootless variant: `...:16-rootless` (data dir `/var/lib/gitea`, UID/GID 1000).
48: - Note: the `:16-rootless` variant stores data under `/var/lib/gitea`, so if you switch from the standard image you must change the volume mount from `/data` to `/var/lib/gitea` (the `/data` mountPath in the manifest below is correct for the non-rootless `:16` image).
49: 
50: ### k3s deployment
51: 
52: Example — abstract (raw manifests; a Helm chart wraps the same primitives):
53: 
54: ```yaml
55: apiVersion: v1
56: kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
57: metadata:
58:   name: forgejo-data
59:   namespace: forgejo
60: spec:
61:   storageClassName: longhorn
62:   accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
63:   resources:
64:     requests:
65:       storage: 20Gi
66: ---
67: apiVersion: apps/v1
68: kind: Deployment
69: metadata:
70:   name: forgejo
71:   namespace: forgejo
72: spec:
73:   replicas: 1
74:   selector: { matchLabels: { app: forgejo } }
75:   template:
76:     metadata:
77:       labels: { app: forgejo }
78:     spec:
79:       containers:
80:         - name: forgejo
81:           image: codeberg.org/forgejo/forgejo:16
82:           ports:
83:             - containerPort: 3000   # web UI + git HTTP
84:             - containerPort: 22     # git over SSH
85:           volumeMounts:
86:             - { name: data, mountPath: /data }
87:           env:
88:             - { name: FORGEJO__server__ROOT_URL, value: "https://git.homelab.local/" }
89:       volumes:
90:         - name: data
91:           persistentVolumeClaim: { claimName: forgejo-data }
92: ---
93: apiVersion: v1
94: kind: Service
95: metadata:
96:   name: forgejo-http
97:   namespace: forgejo
98: spec:
99:   selector: { app: forgejo }
100:   ports:
101:     - { name: http, port: 3000, targetPort: 3000 }
102: ```

104: The Ingress is the `forgejo-ingress` resource shown in
105: `./02_Knowledge/technologies/kubernetes/concepts/ingress.md` — Traefik routes
106: `git.homelab.local` to `forgejo-http:3000` and terminates HTTPS there.

108: ### Configuration (`app.ini` and env vars)
109: 
110: | Setting | Purpose |
111: |---|---|
112: | `[server] DOMAIN` / `ROOT_URL` | Hostname and external URL — `ROOT_URL` should be `https://git.homelab.local/` |
113: | `[server] SSH_PORT` | Port for git-over-SSH (e.g. `22` or `2222` behind a host mapping) |
114: | `[database] DB_TYPE` | `sqlite3` (default), `mysql`, or `postgres` |
115: | `[service] DISABLE_REGISTRATION` | Block public sign-up (see the security note) |
116: | `[actions]` | Enable/disable Forgejo Actions |
117: | `[security] SECRET_KEY` | Instance secret; generate a random value on first install |

120: `FORGEJO__server__ROOT_URL=https://git.homelab.local/`; values can only be added
121: via env vars, never removed — removal requires editing `app.ini`.

124: 
125: - **SQLite** is the default and is enough for a single-owner homelab instance;
126:   the database file lives on the data volume.
127: - **PostgreSQL / MySQL** are supported for heavier instances; point
128:   `[database] DB_TYPE/HOST/NAME/USER/PASSWD` at the DB service.
129: 
130: ### Storage

132: - All repository data, LFS, and uploads live under the mounted volume; on k3s
133:   that is the Longhorn PVC (`./02_Knowledge/technologies/kubernetes/longhorn/storage.md`).
